app.name: Riverside Orders
app.summary: Riverside Orders is the back office of an online shop. It takes the orders the shop's website sends, checks and confirms them, takes the payment, and hands each order to the warehouse until it is shipped. Clerks work the order queue, warehouse staff pick and pack, and the finance team follows invoices and refunds. Customers never see it; they only get the e-mails it sends.
app.story:
An order starts on the shop's website, which posts it to `Orders.submitOrder` the moment the customer presses Pay. Riverside Orders looks the customer up by e-mail address, registers a new one when nobody matches, and asks the payment provider to authorise the amount. An order whose payment is refused never reaches a clerk; the customer is told at once and the order is closed as cancelled.

An authorised order is placed in the confirmation queue. A clerk checks the address and the lines, and confirms it. Confirming decides which warehouse ships it: the one in the customer's region when it has every line in stock, otherwise the central warehouse, otherwise a supplier who promises delivery within five days. When none of the three can, the order is back-ordered and the customer is asked whether to wait.

Once a warehouse holds the stock, the payment is captured and an invoice is written. A job retries captures that failed, three times over a day; after the third failure the order is put on hold for the finance team. The warehouse then picks, packs and ships the order, the carrier's tracking number is stored on it, and the customer gets the shipping e-mail.

Returns come back through the same back office. A clerk registers the returned parcel, the warehouse checks its condition, and the finance team refunds the amount the condition allows. Every e-mail the application sends is logged in `Notifications.MailLog`, which is where support looks first when a customer says nothing arrived.

audience.what: Work the confirmation queue: check each new order's address and lines, confirm it, and answer customers about back-orders and returns.
Pick, pack and ship the orders assigned to their warehouse, and check the condition of returned parcels.
Follow invoices, payments on hold and refunds, and close the month against the accounting system.
Manage users and roles, the warehouses and the e-mail templates.

processes.name: Placing and confirming an order
processes.summary: The website sends an order, the application authorises the payment, and a clerk confirms it; confirming chooses the warehouse that ships it, or back-orders it when none can.
processes.story:
The case starts when the customer presses Pay on the shop's website. The website posts the order to `Orders.submitOrder`, which looks the customer up by e-mail address in `Customers.findCustomer`. A customer nobody matches is registered on the spot by `Customers.registerCustomer`, with the address from the order as their first delivery address.

The application then asks the payment provider to authorise the amount (`Billing.authorisePayment`). A refusal ends the case: the order is saved with the status Cancelled, and the customer gets the refusal e-mail. An authorised order is saved as Awaiting confirmation and appears in the clerks' queue on `Orders.OrderList`.

A clerk opens it on `Orders.OrderDetail`, checks the address and the lines, and presses Confirm, which runs `Orders.confirmOrder`. Confirming tries three sources in turn, each by its own rule in `Warehouse.reserveStock`: the regional warehouse of the customer's postcode, when it holds every line; the central warehouse; and the preferred supplier, when its promised delivery is five days or less. The first that fits holds the stock.

When none fits, the order is set to Back-ordered and the customer is asked by e-mail whether to wait or cancel. Otherwise the order becomes Confirmed and moves on to payment and invoicing.

The clerk confirms the order

processes.name: Taking the payment and invoicing
processes.summary: When the stock is held, the application captures the authorised payment and writes the invoice; captures that fail are retried by a job, and an order is put on hold after the third failure.
processes.story:
Payment starts as soon as a warehouse holds the stock for a confirmed order. `Billing.capturePayment` asks the payment provider to capture the amount authorised when the order was placed. A successful capture writes an invoice with the next number from the invoice series (`Billing.createInvoice`) and records the payment on it.

A capture can fail for reasons the application cannot see: an expired authorisation, a card blocked since. The failure is recorded on `Billing.Payment` with the provider's reason, and the order stays Confirmed.

The job `Billing.retryFailedPayments` runs every four hours and tries each failed capture again, three times at most. After the third failure the order is set to On hold and appears on the finance team's list on `Billing.InvoiceList`, where someone contacts the customer. The provider also calls back the application's webhook when a capture settles; `Billing.handlePaymentWebhook` matches the call to the payment and marks it settled.

processes.name: Picking and shipping
processes.summary: Warehouse staff pick and pack each paid order on the pick list, book the carrier, and the customer gets the shipping e-mail with the tracking number.
processes.story:
A paid order appears on `Warehouse.PickList` of the warehouse that holds its stock. Warehouse staff pick the lines, pack the parcel and press Ship, which runs `Warehouse.shipOrder`.

Shipping books the parcel with the carrier (`Warehouse.bookCarrier`), stores the tracking number on `Warehouse.Shipment`, takes the shipped quantities off the stock, and sets the order to Shipped. `Notifications.sendShippingMail` sends the customer the tracking link.

Every night `Warehouse.nightlyStockSync` compares the stock with the warehouse's own counts and corrects the difference.

steps.text: A paid order appears on the pick list of the warehouse that holds its stock
Warehouse staff pick the lines and pack the parcel
Warehouse staff press Ship, and the application books the carrier
The application stores the tracking number and takes the quantities off the stock
The customer gets the shipping e-mail with the tracking link

processes.name: Returns and refunds
processes.summary: A clerk registers a returned parcel, the warehouse checks its condition, and the finance team refunds what the condition allows; returns after 30 days are refused.
processes.story:
A return starts when a parcel arrives back at a warehouse. A clerk finds the order and registers the return on `Orders.OrderDetail`, which runs `Orders.registerReturn`. A return more than 30 days after delivery is refused, and the customer is told why.

Warehouse staff check the condition of each line. An unused line is refunded in full and goes back to stock; a damaged line is refunded at half its price and written off. `Billing.refundPayment` asks the payment provider for the refund and writes a credit note against the invoice.

The application refunds each line by its condition and writes a credit note

diagram.step: Checks the condition of each line

Refunds in full, puts it back in stock

parts.name: Orders
parts.summary: The heart of the application: orders and their lines, the confirmation queue, the order's status from placed to shipped, and returns.
parts.story:
Every order lives here, from the moment the website sends it to the moment it is shipped or returned. The module owns the order's status and is the only place that should change it; the other modules ask it to.

Clerks work in its two screens: the queue of orders awaiting confirmation and the order itself, where they confirm it, cancel it or register a return.

A job closes orders whose payment was authorised but never captured within 14 days.

notes.title: Layout
items: Services that change an order end in `Order`; the status is changed only through `Orders.changeStatus`.
Each screen's actions sit in a file of the same name.

parts.name: Customers
parts.summary: Customers and their delivery addresses, found by e-mail address and registered on their first order.
parts.story:
A customer is found by e-mail address and registered on the first order nobody matches. The module keeps the delivery addresses and the region each postcode belongs to, which the warehouse rules use.

Clerks correct an address on the customer's screen when a parcel comes back undelivered.

parts.name: Billing
parts.summary: Payments, invoices and refunds: authorises and captures each order's payment, writes invoices and credit notes, and retries captures that failed.
parts.story:
Billing talks to the payment provider in both directions: it asks for authorisations, captures and refunds, and receives the provider's webhook when a capture settles.

Invoices take their number from one series per year. Credit notes refer to the invoice they correct.

The finance team works on the invoice list, which also shows orders on hold.

notes.title: Talking to the payment provider
notes.text: Every call goes through `PaymentConnector`, the vendor's client. Its settings are read once at start-up; a changed key needs a restart.

parts.name: Warehouse
parts.summary: Stock per warehouse, the rules that choose which warehouse ships an order, the pick list, shipments and the carrier booking.
parts.story:
Each warehouse keeps its own stock of each item. When a clerk confirms an order, the module tries the regional warehouse, the central one and the preferred supplier in turn, and reserves the stock in the first that can ship every line.

Warehouse staff work on the pick list and ship from it; shipping books the carrier and stores the tracking number.

parts.name: Notifications
parts.summary: Every e-mail the application sends — confirmations, refusals, back-order questions, shipping and refunds — from templates, each one logged.
parts.story: Notifications renders an e-mail from its template, sends it through the mail service and logs it in `Notifications.MailLog`. Support looks there first when a customer says nothing arrived.

parts.name: PaymentConnector
parts.summary: The payment provider's client, taken unchanged from the vendor.

open: Where the application is hosted, and how many instances run, cannot be told from the source.
Which database it uses in production: the source names a driver, the connection is set per environment.
Whether staff sign in through a company identity provider: the source checks a session, not where it came from.
Whether the nightly stock sync, switched off in the source, runs in production.

access.name: Missing access checks
access.text: Logic that acts on any record without checking who calls it.

secrets.name: Secrets in the source
secrets.text: Keys and passwords written where anyone with the source can read them.

logic.name: Logic and data errors
logic.text: Conditions and calculations that give the wrong answer in some cases.

silent.name: Errors that vanish
silent.text: Failures caught and dropped, so nobody learns something went wrong.

loops.name: Saves in loops
loops.text: Records saved one at a time inside a loop: slow, and half done when one fails.

schedule.name: Relies on switched-off jobs
schedule.text: Work that depends on scheduled jobs switched off in the source.

dead.name: Unused or duplicated
dead.text: Code nothing uses, or the same logic kept twice.

hardcoded.name: Values written into code
hardcoded.text: Values that belong in configuration or constants.

risks.title: Any signed-in user can confirm or cancel any order
risks.detail: `Orders.confirmOrder` and `Orders.cancelOrder` check that a session exists, not that its user is a clerk. A warehouse or finance account can call them directly and change an order's course, although no screen of theirs offers the buttons.
risks.fix: Check the Clerk role at the start of both services, the way `Orders.registerReturn` already does.

risks.title: The payment provider's live key is written in the source
risks.detail: The key `PaymentConnector` uses in production is a constant in the Billing module's settings file. Anyone who can read the repository can take payments and refunds in the shop's name.
risks.fix: Read the key from the environment, and have the provider replace the key that was committed.

risks.title: The payment webhook accepts calls without checking the signature
risks.detail: `Billing.handlePaymentWebhook` marks a payment settled on any call that names a known reference. Someone who learns a reference can mark an unpaid order as paid.
risks.fix: Verify the provider's signature header before reading the event.

risks.title: A partly stocked regional warehouse is skipped even when the rest is central
risks.detail: The warehouse rules need one warehouse to hold every line. An order whose lines are split between the regional and the central warehouse goes to the supplier or is back-ordered, although both together could ship it.
risks.fix: Decide with the business whether split shipments are allowed; if they are, add the rule before the supplier's.

risks.title: A failed e-mail is logged as sent
risks.detail: `Notifications.sendOrderMail` writes the log entry before the mail service answers and catches its error without changing the entry. Support then tells a customer an e-mail went out that never did.
risks.fix: Write the log entry after the mail service answers, with `accepted` set from the answer.

risks.title: The stock is never corrected while the nightly sync is switched off
risks.detail: `Warehouse.nightlyStockSync` is switched off in the source. Nothing else corrects the stock against the warehouses' counts, so the warehouse rules work on numbers that drift.
risks.fix: Confirm whether the job runs in production; if it does not, switch it on or document who corrects the stock.

risks.title: Order lines are saved one at a time
risks.detail: `Orders.submitOrder` saves each line inside the loop that creates it. An order with many lines is slow, and a failure halfway leaves half an order.
risks.fix: Create the lines in the loop and save them together after it, in the same transaction as the order.

risks.title: A digest service nothing calls
risks.detail: `Notifications.legacyDigest` is not called from any service, screen or job.
risks.fix: Remove it, after checking that no report outside the application calls it by name.

risks.title: The 30-day return window and the 5-day supplier promise are written into code
risks.detail: Both limits are literals in the services that apply them. Changing either means a release.
risks.fix: Move both into the settings, with today's values as defaults.

quality.label: Services nothing reaches
quality.sub: No caller, no screen, no job, no endpoint
quality.explain: A service counted here is not called by any other service, not started from a screen, a job or an endpoint. Code that only a script outside the application calls by name shows up here too, so check before removing it.

rule.quote: Remove code that nothing calls once you have checked that nothing outside the repository uses it.

quality.label: Services over 15 steps
quality.sub: Measured on the steps each service takes
quality.explain: Long services are harder to read and to test. The count says nothing about whether the length is justified: a validation that checks twenty fields is long by nature.

quality.label: Jobs switched off
quality.explain: A job switched off in the source may still run in production, where the schedule is set per environment. This is what the source says, not what runs.

quality.label: Services without a role check
quality.sub: Started from a screen or an endpoint
quality.explain: Each service a person or another system can start should check who is calling. Services only other services call are left out. A check done by a shared middleware the analysis could not follow would also show up here.

rule.quote: Every service started from outside checks the caller's role before it reads or changes data.

quality.label: Names outside the convention
quality.explain: Every service name starts with a verb in camel case, as the team's guideline asks.

rule.quote: Service names start with a verb: submitOrder, not orderSubmit.

where.place: Only in `Orders.changeStatus`, which also writes the history record. `Warehouse.shipOrder` and `Orders.confirmOrder` call it.
`Warehouse.reserveStock`: three rules tried in turn — regional, central, supplier.

where.topic: Why a customer says no e-mail arrived
where.place: `Notifications.MailLog`; but see `R-005` before trusting its `accepted` column.

where.topic: Where the payment provider is called
where.place: Only through `PaymentConnector`, from the Billing services.

conventions.meaning: A service a person or a system starts; checks the caller's role.
Started by the job runner on a schedule.
Renders a template, sends it and logs it.

pitfalls: Changing an order's status anywhere but `Orders.changeStatus` skips the history record, and the finance team's month-end report misses the order.
`Warehouse.reserveStock` captures the payment as its last step; a change that reserves stock elsewhere must capture it too.
The payment provider's settings are read once at start-up; a changed key needs a restart.
Invoice numbers come from one series per year: never create an invoice outside `Billing.createInvoice`.
